_notes: The author record for pauldejong.com. Single source of truth for everything about Paul G. de Jong as an author: names, bios, headshots, publisher, contacts, profiles, press material.

build.py reads it, exposes it to every template as `author`, and writes it into: the <head> of every page (titles, Open Graph, JSON-LD Person), the About page, the author section on the homepage, the press kit at /press/, and METADATA.md at the repo root.
Book data lives in series.json. METADATA.md is generated from both files on every build; edit the JSON, never the Markdown.

Bios are third person so the name appears in the text (search engines and AI crawlers rank the About page and homepage for the name from the body text, not from the frontmatter). Keep them in Paul's voice: plain words, no cliche, no fancy wording, no em dashes.

headshots: the first entry marked primary is used on the About page, the homepage and in the JSON-LD Person. Every entry is listed on the press kit with its pixel size. Put files under static/images/author/. The entry present now is the interim 600 x 600 portrait; replace or add the chosen headshots when the review by friends is done. A press headshot should be at least 1300 px on the long side.
profiles: every URL goes into the JSON-LD sameAs list, so each one must be the author's own page, not a site homepage. Leave a value empty to leave it out everywhere.
seo.home_title is the <title> of the homepage: money keywords first, then the name. Other pages use '<page title> | Paul G. de Jong' unless the page title already contains the name.

sites.alternate_domains: name domains Paul owns (paulgdejong.com, pgdejong.com; Cloudflare Registrar since 2026-11-09, renew 2028-04-26), 301 to pauldejong.com; each goes into the JSON-LD Person sameAs list. sites.series_domains: astronomyshockingtwist.com and astronomysshockingtwist.com (Cloudflare Registrar since 2026-11-09, renew 2027-10-11), 301 to /series/, not in the Person sameAs. Recorded in METADATA.md.

bios.long is the contributor bio filed at Bowker on 2026-11-10 (244 words); it is the canonical long bio and must stay word for word identical with Bowker, KDP and the Library of Congress record. The hydrogen body is the International Association for Hydrogen Energy (IAHE), not 'Hydrogen Energy Society'.

bios.one_line: Paul G. de Jong is the author of Orbital Ring Engineering and the Astronomy's Shocking Twist series: five engineering textbooks and five hard science fiction novels about mass transit to space.
bios.short: Paul G. de Jong writes at the intersection of physics, electronics and engineering, with three decades of work in medical ultrasound, hydrogen energy, software, audio and a home physics lab. Orbital Ring Engineering is his three-volume engineering treatment of space mass transit infrastructure: orbital rings, mass drivers and space elevators. His threshold for suspension of disbelief is very low, and the technical series arose from a desire for more truly hard science fiction.
bios.medium:
Paul G. de Jong is the author of Orbital Ring Engineering, a three-volume engineering treatment of orbital rings, mass drivers and space elevators, and of Why Space, the economic case for mass transit to space written for the general reader. Both belong to Astronomy's Shocking Twist, a ten-book project: five technical books written to serve as undergraduate textbooks and five hard science fiction novels set in the world the technical books describe. The novels obey the known laws of physics. People live normal lifespans, propulsion is limited by the power that can be produced, materials are limited to reasonable extrapolations of current research, heat has to go somewhere, and every trajectory is calculated with real orbital mechanics.

De Jong studied electronics and physics at Heald Institute of Technology, Ohlone College, UC Berkeley and the University of Amsterdam. He has worked as an electronics technician in medical ultrasound, in hydrogen energy when it was still a fringe topic, and as an inventor and software entrepreneur in San Francisco. His derivations are done in MathCAD and checked against open-source Python simulations that readers can download and run.
bios.long:
Paul G. de Jong is a Dutch-American author and entrepreneur. He studied physics at the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Amsterdam, where he took an early interest in chaos theory. In the 1990s he was a member of the International Association for Hydrogen Energy and attended its 10th World Hydrogen Energy Conference in Florida in 1994.

Settling in San Francisco in 1997, he founded several software companies: AnyTaxi, a direct user-to-provider dispatch system; Club Clock, an automated tour-booking platform; and KaraokeListMaker, a karaoke-hosting system with mobile requests.

In the mid-2010s, Andy Weir's The Martian and Isaac Arthur's YouTube channel, Science & Futurism with Isaac Arthur, brought him back to physics, and Gerard K. O'Neill's The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space set the direction. The storyline of the ten-book series Astronomy's Shocking Twist took its final shape in 2024.

During the COVID years he worked through electromagnetism, nuclear physics, plasma physics and superconductivity, and designed a high-power ion accelerator, the THOR Drive, the subject of the series' second technical book.

Orbital Ring Engineering, in three volumes, is the first of the five technical books. It applies decades of problem-solving as an entrepreneur to an orbital ring, a megastructure he expects to be built within the next 100 to 200 years.

talking_points: What an orbital ring is, in one minute: a cable in orbit moving faster than orbital velocity, a stationary casing riding on it, anchor lines tying it to the ground, and a mass driver on top that throws spacecraft to the Moon and Mars. No rockets, no fuel, no countdown.
Why mass transit to space is an engineering question, not a physics question: every part of the ring uses known physics and materials that exist or are reasonable extrapolations of current research.
The heat problem: heat dissipation, not thrust, is the limit on space propulsion and on any megastructure, and what that does to the design.
The power budget: how much power an orbital ring needs, where it comes from, and why the same ring can power the planet.
Hard science fiction in the strictest sense: known laws, real materials, normal lifespans, real orbital mechanics, and why the fiction gets better when the author is not allowed to cheat.
Writing a textbook and a novel series at the same time, and how each one changes the other.
Showing the work: every number traceable to a paper, a calculation in the book, or open-source code the reader can run.
Using AI tools in technical writing without letting them do the engineering.
From Isaac Arthur's YouTube channel to a ten-book series: how a hobby of thinking about megastructures became a full-time project.
Why the 2025 first edition of Orbital Ring Engineering was replaced by three volumes, and what a complete design review of an orbital ring looks like.
